title: AC/DC on a Budget -- Alternating Sparse Phases
claim: Reintroduced out-of-mask parameters sit near zero yet receive disproportionately large gradients during dense phases, which drives rewiring.
layout: 2x4 grid of scatter plots, columns are alternating phases, rows are start/end
description: A shared legend on top shows blue dots for out-of-mask weights, orange dots for in-mask weights, and a dashed blue line for the magnitude threshold. Below it is a 2x4 grid of scatter plots with weights on the x-axis and gradients on the y-axis. Columns are titled Dense 54->64, Sparse 64->74, Dense 74->84 and Sparse 84->94. The top row is the start of each phase and the bottom row is the end. In the dense columns, a tall blue vertical cloud of out-of-mask weights near zero shows large gradients, on top of a flat orange horizontal band. In the sparse columns, orange points spread on either side of dashed threshold lines, with a gap in the middle. The y-axis scales differ widely between panels. The eye goes first to the blue spikes in the dense panels.
caption: Gradient--weight dynamics across AC/DC phases. Gradient versus weight scatter plots for layer4.0.conv2 of a 90% sparse ResNet18 on CIFAR100. Top and bottom rows show the beginning and end of each phase, respectively. During sparse phases, many active weights move toward small magnitude and small gradient. During dense phases, many reintroduced out-of-mask weights remain near zero but receive large gradients.
abstract: State-of-the-art neural network sparsification relies on alternating dense and sparse training phases. While computationally expensive, dense phases are critical for performance. Our empirical analysis reveals the mechanics behind this gain: upon reintroduction, previously masked parameters receive disproportionately large gradients that drive essential mask rewiring and parameter sign-flipping. Building on these insights, we optimize the performance-to-FLOPs Pareto frontier through three innovations: (1) zero-initializing masked parameters during dense phases to promote relevant sign flips, (2) shortening dense phases, and (3) replacing the dense phase entirely with a sparse rewiring phase that updates only the active mask and a small, high-gradient fraction of out-of-mask weights. Evaluated on CIFAR100 and ImageNet, our variant ARC (Alternating Rewiring Compression) matches baseline AC/DC performance at a fraction of the computational cost, establishing a superior performance-to-FLOPs frontier also compared to standard sparse-to-sparse algorithms. Experiments with GPT-2 on OpenWebText further show improvements in validation perplexity and average zero-shot performance
